words.definition: A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given premises.
words.example: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal — that syllogism is the textbook example.
words.mnemonic: SILL-o-gism: picture two premises sitting on a window SILL, and the conclusion dropping off the edge (Greek syllogismos, 'a reckoning together').

words.definition: Relating to formal reasoning that derives a conclusion from two stated premises.
words.example: Her essay advanced in tight syllogistic steps, each claim resting squarely on the two before it.
words.mnemonic: Same root as its parent form; the suffix '-istic' means 'in the style of' — the style of stacking two premises to force a result.

words.definition: Inquiry that pursues truth by weighing opposing arguments against each other.
words.example: Through a patient dialectic of thesis and counter-thesis, the seminar edged toward a shared view.
words.mnemonic: DIA- ('across') + -lect ('speak'): two voices speaking across each other. Sounds like 'dial-a-tick' — dialing back and forth between two sides.

words.definition: Using arguments that seem clever and plausible but are actually misleading or false.
words.example: The lawyer's sophistic patter dazzled the jury until the prosecutor exposed the hollow logic beneath it.
words.mnemonic: The ancient Sophists were paid to win arguments, not find truth — 'so-FIST-ic' = a slick fist of fake reasoning.

words.definition: A person who uses subtle, often misleading reasoning, especially about matters of right and wrong.
words.example: A practiced casuist, he could justify almost any broken promise with a tidy little exception.
words.mnemonic: CASE + -ist: one who splits every moral CASE into finer and finer hairs until the rule quietly vanishes.

words.definition: A flawed piece of reasoning made without any intent to deceive.
words.example: His conclusion collapsed on inspection — a paralogism that quietly confused correlation with cause.
words.mnemonic: PARA- ('beside, off') + logic: reasoning that slips off to the side of true logic — like a line that looks parallel but veers away.

words.definition: Needlessly repeating the same idea in different words, or true merely by its own terms.
words.example: Saying 'a free gift' is tautological, since a gift is by definition already free.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'tauto' means 'the same' — picture a taut rope pulled tight between two identical ends, looping back on itself.

words.definition: Established as certain beyond any possible doubt.
words.example: Mathematicians treat 2 + 2 = 4 as apodictic — no future evidence could ever overturn it.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-po-DIC-tate': it dictates a truth you simply cannot argue back against (Greek apodeiktikos, 'capable of proof').

words.definition: Serving to test something or to furnish evidence in support of a claim.
words.example: The DNA match was highly probative, tipping the jury decisively toward a guilty verdict.
words.mnemonic: PROBATIVE ~ PROBE: it probes a claim and thereby proves it (Latin probare, 'to test, prove').

words.definition: Bringing an issue to a final and conclusive settlement.
words.example: One overlooked receipt proved dispositive, ending the whole dispute before lunch.
words.mnemonic: Think DISPOSE: a dispositive fact disposes of the question entirely, leaving nothing left to argue.

words.definition: To insert extra material into a text, or to estimate a value lying between known ones.
words.example: A later scribe seems to have interpolated a paragraph the original author never wrote.
words.mnemonic: INTER- ('between') + '-pole': you plant a new pole between two poles already standing.

words.definition: Reasoning from general rules toward a specific, logically guaranteed conclusion.
words.example: Starting from established physical laws, she reached her answer by purely deductive steps.
words.mnemonic: DE- ('down') + duce ('lead'): you lead the truth DOWN from a broad rule to a single case.

words.definition: Reasoning from particular observations toward a broader, probable generalization.
words.example: After watching a thousand sunrises, he drew the inductive conclusion that the sun rises every day.
words.mnemonic: IN- ('into') + duce ('lead'): many small facts lead INTO one big rule — the reverse of leading down.

words.definition: Relating to knowledge and the grounds on which we claim to know things.
words.example: The witness's admission created serious epistemic doubt about everything else she had claimed.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'episteme' means knowledge (the root of epistemology) — hear the STEM in epi-STEM-ic: the stem of what you know.

words.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, sources, and limits of human knowledge.
words.example: Her epistemology led her to distrust any claim that couldn't be tested or observed firsthand.
words.mnemonic: Greek epistēmē (knowledge) + -logy (study). Hear 'epi-STEM': the study of how we know what we know.

words.definition: Coinciding with fact; genuinely truthful and accurate.
words.example: The witness gave a veridical account that matched every detail the security cameras had captured.
words.mnemonic: Latin veritas = truth, same root as 'verify'. A veridical dream is one that comes true.

words.definition: Impossible to deny or dispute because it is so clearly certain.
words.example: The DNA match was incontrovertible, and even the defense lawyers stopped arguing.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + contro-vert (turn against, as in 'controversy') — you can't turn it around on itself.

words.definition: Impossible to refute or argue against.
words.example: She built an irrefragable case, brick by brick, until no one could poke a single hole in it.
words.mnemonic: ir- (not) + think 'FRAG' — an argument that cannot be fragmented or broken apart.

words.definition: A statement taken as true and used as the basis for reasoning or a conclusion.
words.example: His whole business plan rested on the premise that interest rates would stay low.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + mise (put/send) — what you put down before the conclusion. It comes first.

words.definition: A statement that follows logically and easily from one already proven.
words.example: Higher wages were a welcome corollary of the region's sudden economic boom.
words.mnemonic: From Latin corolla, 'little garland' — a bonus wreath that comes attached. Picture a 'collar' that follows the shirt.

words.definition: Regarded as obviously true and needing no proof.
words.example: It is axiomatic in medicine that prevention costs far less than a cure.
words.mnemonic: From 'axiom' (Greek axios = worthy). Say 'axe-io-MATIC': a truth so solid it's automatic.

words.definition: A clever argument that seems sound but is deliberately deceptive or false.
words.example: The salesman's pitch was pure sophism, dressing a bad deal in flawless-sounding logic.
words.mnemonic: Greek sophos = wise (as in 'sophisticated'), but it only looks wise — hear 'so-phony'.

words.definition: A disturbed mental state marked by confusion, restlessness, and sometimes hallucinations.
words.example: By nightfall the fever had risen so high that she slipped into delirium, muttering to people who weren't there.
words.mnemonic: Latin delirare = to go off the furrow (de- + lira, the plowed ridge) — the mind leaves its track.

words.definition: Suffering confused, incoherent thinking, often from fever; also wildly and joyfully excited.
words.example: The fans were delirious when the final whistle confirmed the championship.
words.mnemonic: Same 'off the furrow' root as its noun cousin — a serious fever makes you 'de-LEER-ious'.

words.definition: Mentally disturbed to the point of behaving in a wild or irrational way.
words.example: The letters grew stranger each week, until they read like the work of a deranged mind.
words.mnemonic: de- (undo) + range/arrange — someone whose thoughts are un-arranged, knocked completely out of order.

words.definition: Behaving in a mad, irrational, or wildly foolish manner.
words.example: He drove with a demented recklessness, weaving through traffic at twice the speed limit.
words.mnemonic: de- (away) + -ment- (mind, as in 'mental') — the mind driven away. Think 'de-minded'.

words.definition: A progressive decline in memory and reasoning caused by disease of the brain.
words.example: As the dementia advanced, her grandfather could no longer recognize his own children.
words.mnemonic: de- (away) + -ment- (mind) + -ia (condition) — a condition of the mind slipping away.

words.definition: Extreme foolishness or madness; a wildly senseless act or idea.
words.example: Spending the entire year's budget on fireworks was sheer lunacy.
words.mnemonic: Latin luna = moon; once blamed on the full moon — picture 'moon-madness'.

words.definition: A state of abnormally elevated mood and energy, or an intense obsessive enthusiasm.
words.example: Tulip mania gripped the country until fortunes were traded for a single bulb.
words.mnemonic: Greek mania = madness, sharing a root with 'maniac' — an unstoppable high or craving.

words.definition: Marked by frantic, uncontrolled excitement or wildly restless energy.
words.example: He scrubbed the entire house at 3 a.m. in a manic burst that left everyone bewildered.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'panic' — a panicked mind races and can't sit still.

words.definition: A state of wild, uncontrolled excitement or agitation.
words.example: The shoppers descended on the half-price rack in a frenzy, grabbing armfuls before anyone else could.
words.mnemonic: Picture sharks in a feeding frenzy — thrashing water, all instinct, no control.

words.definition: Marked by fast, chaotic, and disordered activity.
words.example: The kitchen turned frenetic during the dinner rush, cooks shouting over clattering pans.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'frantic' inside it — from Greek 'phren' (mind), an out-of-mind pace.

words.definition: Overwhelming, uncontrollable fear or emotion that often spreads through a group.
words.example: When the alarm blared, hysteria swept the theater and people trampled one another at the doors.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'his-teary-a' — everyone in tears and out of their minds.

words.definition: Wildly emotional and completely out of control.
words.example: She grew hysterical when the news came, sobbing and shaking so hard she couldn't speak.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'hysteria' — 'his-teary-cal', too upset to hold it together.

words.definition: Extremely worried, upset, or emotionally distressed.
words.example: The distraught father searched the crowded fairground for his missing daughter.
words.mnemonic: 'Distracted' plus 'fraught' — so troubled your mind is pulled apart.

words.definition: Marked by feverish intensity or nervous, restless excitement.
words.example: In the febrile final hours before the vote, campaigners barely slept and jumped at every phone call.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'febris' (fever) — a febrile brow burns hot.

words.definition: Having extreme, fanatical, or uncontrolled feelings or enthusiasm.
words.example: He's a rabid supporter who paints his whole body in team colors for every match.
words.mnemonic: Think of an animal with rabies — foaming, frothing, out of control.

words.definition: Believing things that are clearly untrue despite strong evidence against them.
words.example: He was delusional, certain that TV anchors were sending him coded personal messages.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'illusion' inside it — living in an illusion your mind treats as real.

words.definition: A false perception of something that is not actually present.
words.example: Feverish and dehydrated, the hiker had a hallucination of a shimmering lake in the empty desert.
words.mnemonic: 'Hall-you-see-nation' — you see a whole nation crowding an empty hall.

words.definition: Extreme, irrational distrust or suspicion of other people.
words.example: His paranoia grew until he taped over every webcam and suspected even his own family.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'para' (beside) + 'nous' (mind) — your mind slips beside itself into suspicion.

words.definition: An excessive preoccupation with one single idea or subject.
words.example: Captain Ahab's monomania drove him to chase one white whale to his own destruction.
words.mnemonic: 'Mono' (one) + 'mania' (obsession) — a single fixation that crowds out everything else.

words.definition: Not guided by reason or sound judgment.
words.example: She has an irrational fear of butterflies, even though she knows they can't hurt her.
words.mnemonic: The prefix 'ir-' means 'not' — it flips the switch: not thinking straight.

words.definition: The quality of being wildly unreasonable, silly, or senseless.
words.example: The absurdity of two grown men fighting over a parking spot finally made them both laugh.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'absurdus' (out of tune) — an idea so off-key it collapses; hear 'ab-sturdy', not sturdy enough to stand.

words.definition: Having no meaning or logic; foolish and utterly absurd.
words.example: His nonsensical directions told us to turn left at a corner that doesn't even exist.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'non + sense + ical' — literally not making sense.

words.definition: The state of speech or thought lacking logical connection and being impossible to follow.
words.example: By the third hour of the fever, his mumbled sentences dissolved into pure incoherence, and no one could follow him.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + cohere (stick together): thoughts that refuse to stick together.

words.definition: Departing markedly from what is normal, usual, or expected.
words.example: The lab flagged one aberrant reading that sat far outside every other result on the chart.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'ab-errant': an errant knight who wanders off the correct path.

words.definition: A contagious viral disease of dogs and other animals, marked by fever and coughing.
words.example: The shelter quarantined the litter after a puppy showed the fever and twitching that signal distemper.
words.mnemonic: dis- + temper: a body knocked out of its proper temper (balance) by illness.

words.definition: Mentally unbalanced; behaving in a wild, irrational way.
words.example: After days without sleep, she started laughing at nothing and muttering to the walls, completely unhinged.
words.mnemonic: A door off its hinges swings wildly and uncontrollably — so does a mind off its hinges.

words.definition: To leave someone so surprised or confused that they cannot think how to react.
words.example: The witness's calm confession seemed to nonplus the prosecutor, who paused and shuffled his notes in silence.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "non-plus" — your brain can add nothing more; the math of thought stalls at zero.

words.definition: To make someone unable to think clearly, often through shock or boredom.
words.example: The lecture droned on so long that it stupefied the entire class into glassy-eyed silence.
words.mnemonic: 'stupe-' echoes 'stupid' + -fy (to make): to make the mind stupid and dazed.

words.definition: To cause someone to lose their sense of direction or grasp of surroundings.
words.example: The windowless corridors and identical doors disoriented him until he no longer knew which way led out.
words.mnemonic: dis- (undo) + orient (find your east/bearings): to undo a person's bearings.

words.definition: Smug, complacent foolishness, or a remark showing it.
words.example: His grinning fatuity, boasting about a plan everyone could see would fail, embarrassed the whole table.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'fatuus' (foolish); picture a 'fat-headed' grin too self-satisfied to notice the folly.

words.definition: The quality of being silly, empty, or utterly lacking in substance.
words.example: She could not sit through another dinner of gossip and inanity that added nothing to anyone's life.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'inanis' (empty): an empty-headed comment with nothing inside it.

words.definition: The state of being empty, especially empty of ideas or intelligence.
words.example: Behind his confident smile lay a startling vacuity; he had not one real idea to offer.
words.mnemonic: vacuity = vacuum + -ity: a vacuum sitting where a thought should be.

words.definition: Extremely stupid or foolish.
words.example: Texting while crossing a busy highway is an asinine thing to do.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'asinus' (donkey/ass): acting like a braying, stubborn donkey.

words.definition: Childishly silly and immature.
words.example: The senators traded puerile insults about each other's haircuts instead of debating the budget.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'puer' (boy): behaving like a squabbling little boy.

words.definition: Showing a lack of good sense; unwise or imprudent.
words.example: Announcing the layoffs by mass email the night before the holidays was a deeply injudicious move.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + judicious (like a wise judge): lacking a judge's careful good sense.

words.definition: To use the brain; to think deeply about something.
words.example: Give me a quiet hour to cerebrate on the problem before you ask me for an answer.
words.mnemonic: 'cerebrum' is the brain: to cerebrate is to put your cerebrum to work.

words.definition: To unsettle or fluster someone, disturbing their composure.
words.example: The interviewer's long, unblinking stare disconcerted the candidate into forgetting her rehearsed answer.
words.mnemonic: dis- + concert: when players are no longer 'in concert,' everything feels jarring and off.

words.definition: To talk or move in a rambling, aimless way without any clear purpose.
words.example: Grandpa would maunder on about the weather for a half hour before finally saying why he'd phoned.
words.mnemonic: Sounds almost like 'meander' — a river that maunders wanders with no direction, and so does the talker.

words.definition: Foolishly and completely infatuated with, or devoted to, someone or something.
words.example: He was so besotted with her that he forgot his own address the moment she smiled at him.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'be + sot': a 'sot' is a drunkard, so to be besotted is to be drunk — on love instead of liquor.

words.definition: Absent-minded and inattentive, usually because of worry or anxiety.
words.example: So distrait was the pilot after the phone call that he taxied straight past his own gate.
words.mnemonic: Say it like 'distract' with a French accent — a distrait mind is one that something has already distracted.

words.definition: Impossible to avoid, resist, or escape.
words.example: Once the debts kept mounting, bankruptcy became ineluctable, a wall he simply could not climb over.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'e-luctari', to struggle out, plus 'in-', not — no matter how you struggle, there is no getting out.

words.definition: A shifting, dreamlike sequence of real or imagined figures and images.
words.example: The fever turned his bedroom into a phantasmagoria of melting walls and shadows that whispered his name.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'phantasm' (a ghost or illusion) at the front — picture a whole parade of phantoms drifting past.

words.definition: An unpredictable or capricious change in behavior, mood, or circumstances.
words.example: By some vagary of the postal system, the birthday card finally arrived three years after it was mailed.
words.mnemonic: Same Latin root 'vagari' (to wander) as 'vagabond' — a vagary is a whim that wanders off wherever it likes.

words.definition: To devise or figure out a plan or idea through careful, deliberate thinking.
words.example: She locked herself away for a week to excogitate a way out of the company's debt.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out) + cogitate (to think): to think something OUT.

words.definition: Utterly absurd, contrary to common sense, or ridiculous to the point of disbelief.
words.example: The claim that he swam across the ocean overnight is simply preposterous.
words.mnemonic: Latin prae- (before) + posterus (after): 'before-after,' back-to-front and nonsensical.

words.definition: A sudden, violent outburst of emotion, activity, or a bodily attack.
words.example: At the punchline the whole room collapsed into a paroxysm of helpless laughter.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pair of spasms' — sudden, uncontrollable fits.

words.definition: A serious lack of good judgment, or a costly, senseless act.
words.example: Building a mansion on the crumbling cliff proved to be an expensive folly.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'follow' — blindly following a whim straight into trouble.

words.definition: Excessive, uncritical enthusiasm or devotion, especially toward a religious or political cause.
words.example: His fanaticism for the team drove him to attend every game across three continents.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'fan' — a super-fan whose devotion has spun completely out of proportion.

words.definition: Fanatical, uncompromising devotion to a cause, pursued with relentless intensity.
words.example: The reformer's zealotry alienated even the allies who shared his goals.
words.mnemonic: A 'zealot' guarding a fortress gate, fierce and refusing all compromise.

words.definition: Wildly out of control, frenzied, or destructively enraged.
words.example: When the printer jammed yet again, he went berserk and hurled it out the window.
words.mnemonic: From Norse 'berserkers' — bear-shirted warriors who fought in a wild frenzy.
